title: A Million People Pressed 'Seems Like AI Slop'
hook: LinkedIn gave users a button to flag posts as AI slop. Over a million clicks later, it's a rare public measure of how tired people are of machine-written filler.
key_points: LinkedIn announced a 'Seems like AI slop' report option on July 30, 2026.
Chief product officer Hari Srinivasan said over a million people have clicked it.
The button sits in the three-dot menu on a post, like any other report action.
Crowd flags are a signal, not proof — people can only guess whether a post was AI-written.
It shows platforms now treat 'too much AI content' as a feed-quality problem, not just a labeling one.
content_html: On July 30, 2026, LinkedIn quietly added a "Seems like AI slop" option to the report menu on posts. Three weeks later, chief product officer Hari Srinivasan said more than a million people had used it — a striking number for a feature buried behind a three-dot menu.
extra_html: It's worth being precise about what that number is. The button records suspicion: a reader thought a post looked machine-generated. Nobody, including LinkedIn, can tell from the text alone whether it was. What the count really documents is fatigue — enough of it that a major professional network now treats "too much AI filler" as a feed-quality problem worth instrumenting, alongside the labeling and watermarking efforts elsewhere. The Verge has the details.

related.title: Spotting AI-Made Content
related.hook: There are real tells for AI text and images — but they're fading fast, and 'AI detector' tools are unreliable. The durable skill is judging the source, not squinting at the pixels.

related.title: AI Detectors Are Making Everyone Suspicious of Everyone
related.hook: Tools that claim to spot AI writing are unreliable enough to flag honest work — and the damage isn't just false accusations. It's that nobody trusts anything anymore.

flashcards.prompt: What does LinkedIn's 'Seems like AI slop' button actually measure?
flashcards.back_html: Reader suspicion, not fact — it records that over a million people thought a post looked machine-written, which is a signal rather than proof.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a crowd-sourced 'AI slop' flag a weak way to identify AI-written text?

choices.text: People are guessing from style, and human-written filler can read the same way
Only verified accounts are allowed to use the button
The button deletes the post immediately, so nothing can be checked

flashcards.explanation_html: The flag captures how a post reads to readers. Since bland human writing and AI writing look alike, the signal reflects perception more than origin.
